newsitem.title: UK: Nickel ends down on LME, Inco talks re-starting.
newsitem.headline: Nickel ends down on LME, Inco talks re-starting.

text.p: Nickel prices fell away during late Thursday trading to close at the lows on the LME, as news emerged of talks resuming at strike-bound Inco facilities, traders said.
Most other metals flattered to deceive, with copper and aluminium yet again failing to clear $2,600 and $1,600 respectively, although zinc managed to close firm and near 4-3/4 year highs.
Nickel turned back under the $7,200 level during late kerb trading, against a background of news Inco is to resume talks with unions at Sudbury later on Thursday.
An Inco spokesman said that the talks could go through the weekend, with the expectation of a package at the weekend.
If so, the market is extremely vulnerable on the downside, as this would would remove one of the two supportive props - the other is gas supply threats at Russia's Norilsk.
"What has been surprising is that it has hardly reacted to problems at the world's two biggest producers," said Angus MacMillan of LME trader Billiton Metals Ltd.
Once those factors are out of the way the next move could be to the downside, with charts suggesting $7,000, $6,000 and then $6,400, he said.
Last trade today was at $7,160, down $70 from Wednesday.
Zinc powered up to fresh 4-3/4 year highs, boosted by speculative fund-based buying, with prices getting close to the psychological $1,400 level.
Today's move was largely technical and speculative, although there are solid fundamantal reasons as well with the market expected to be in deficit in 1997 as a whole, analysts said.
Fundamentally, demand seems to be strong, production seems to be nicely balanced, but the Chinese are the wild card," MacMillan said.
"There is the feeling that China may sell more, but not enough to damage an overall deficit market," William Adams of LME trader Rudolf Wolff said.
Last business was at $1,393, just $1 off its peak, and an $18 gain from Wednesday.
Copper again moved above $2,600 for a brief moment, but was again repulsed and spun lower to close at $2,585.50, down $6.50, despite a widening backwardation of $114/119.
Traders said the $2,600 in an obvious level to take profits, as well as short-sell, with the market needing to break $2,610 to find new territory.
Aluminium again picked direction from copper and attempted to take out "big-figure" resistance at $1,600.
But it similarly failed, and slid lower to finish at $1,584, a $9 loss.
"If copper was to go through $2,600 then aluminium would get above $1,600," Adams noted.
Elsewhere in the complex tin closed quietly higher at $5,615, up $35. Lead was also lacklustre and was just $2 up at $626 at the end of the kerb.
The alloy market was indicated at $1,473/75 a tonne, little changed from Wednesday.
--Martin Hayes, London newsroom 44 171 542 8080
